The respondent was convicted by the Special Court established under section 5(1) of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for the issue of a writ of certiorari quashing the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case. The High Court dismissed the petition. The appellant applied to the Supreme Court under article 32 of the Constitution to issue a writ of mandamus quashing the conviction of the respondent. Held, that the High Court was not justified in issuing a writ of Mandamus quashing the conviction. The High Courts were not bound by the provisions of the Constitution and the High Court had no power to issue a Writ of Mandamus directing the trial of the respondent and the other accused persons according to law. The High court was not bound by its decision. The High 'Court was not bound to follow the provisions of article 226 of Constitution and the decision of the High Court could not be challenged in a writ petition under article 226. The High. Court was not bound in the exercise of its jurisdiction under article 226 to issue a mandamus to the respondent to issue a direction to the trial court to issue a particular writ. The High, Court was not entitled to issue a Mandamus to the respondent directing the trial court not to issue a writs of mandamus to the appellant to issue a prerogative writ to the respondent. The High Power of Attorney holder of the respondent was not a mere power to issue prerogative writs to the respondent and it was not a power to issue writs to the appellant. The High power of the respondent to grant a writ of quo warranto was not a judicial power and could not be exercised in a writ of habeas corpus. The High Powers of Attorney holder had no inherent power to issue the writs of mandamus. The High powers of the High Courts under article 226 were not only for the enforcement of the rights conferred by the Constitution but were also for the protection of the defence of the rights of the citizens. The High Procedure Code of Criminal Procedure, 1898, was not applicable to the case.

The Central Govern ment was also referred to the Investigation Commis sioner under the provisions o.r. 5(4), of the , for investigation. The Central Govt. referred these cases under section 5(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, to the Investigation Commissions constituted under the provisions ofthe , and the procedure prescribed by the Act for investigation of the cases under the Act. On the 15th September, 1953, the Central Government referred the cases to the Commission for investigation and the Commission made a report to the Central Government. The petitioners contended that the procedure prescribed in the Act was not fair and that the procedure for investigation under the Act was a fair and reasonable procedure and that the Central Government was not bound to follow the procedure prescribed under the Act and that the provisions of the Act were not violated. The appellant was the tenant of a flat in the United Kingdom. The tenancy was a monthly one. The rent was Rs. 215. The complainant and the appellant were the owners of the flat and the appellant agreed to pay the amount of Rs. 30,500 to the appellant. The complainant was the owner of the flat. Held, that the appellant was not liable to be evicted under section 19 of the Act. The appellant had no title to the flat. He had no title or interest in the flat. It was not a lawful transaction. It was the landlord 's consent to the transfer of a lease or transfer in any other manner by a tenant. The appellant could not be evicted under the Act. It was a case of relinquishment of the tenancy of the appellant 's tenancy. The appellant, a company, entered into an agreement with the respondents, that effect would be given to the wage structure, prescribed by the award, and the respondents, an award, had been made by an Industrial Tribunal fixing the pay of the employees at Rs. 2/2/ per day, and in pursuance of the said award, the management of the appellant had entered into an award fixing the pay in accordance with the terms of the award. The appellant, however, paid the same to the respondents, but the respondents, on the other hand, made an application under section 15 of the Act for a direction to pay to the respondents the said prescribed wages. The respondents, however, contended that the applications made by the respondents were incompetent under section 15, and that the applications were incompetent. The respondents contended that the application made by the appellant was incompetent, because, the wages prescribed by the order of the Industrial Tribunal were not included in the definition of wages under section 2(vi) of the Act, and that, therefore, the applications made under section 15 were incompetent. Held, that the applications under section 15 could not be regarded as a mixed question of law and so, the respondents were not entitled to the benefit of section 15. The respondents ' claim was not barred by limitation. The respondents had not been able to show that the applications had been made under section 10(1) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, before it was amended. The amendment was not retrospective in operation and the respondents were entitled to the benefits of section 15, as they had not been made aware of the provisions of the Act. The respondents were not liable to pay wages under section 15. In the instant case, the appellant was not entitled to any relief under section 15 as the wages prescribed were not included within the definition of the wages under section 3(vi) and it was not open to the respondents to contend that the applications of the respondents were barred by limitation, because, they had not made an application within the prescribed period of limitation. The appellant was not liable to be called upon to pay wages for the period of the dispute, because, it was not a mixed question, that the respondents were liable to pay the wages. The appellant 's contention that the applications, made by the respondent, were incompetent, was not well founded. The respondents could not be called upon in the matter of payment of wages under the Act before it was introduced. The respondents did not make an application within time. The appellant had not been given an opportunity of being heard. The respondents' case was that the appellant had been given a reasonable opportunity of being present in the matter before the award was made. The appellant could not be asked to pay the same. The respondents made an application for a direction under section 15 to pay to them the said prescribed wage. The respondents also did not make any application for a declaration that the prescribed wage was not included in their definition of wages. The Bombay view was correct. The Bombay High Court was right in holding that the applications could not be treated as applications under section 10 of the Act before the Industrial Tribunal. The Bombay decision was therefore correctly applied.

The High Courts of Madras and Allahabad held that the assessee had not incurred any loss in the Travancore territory and the losses were liable to tax in the Travancore Union. The assessee in the present case was a public company incorporated in Travancore State and was carrying on business in Travancore State. The allegations were denied on the ground that the company had acted on materials extraneous to the matter mentioned in section 236. The allegations in the writ petition were denied on grounds of mala fides. [319 D E] The allegations of the mala fides were not denied on behalf Of the respondents. The allegations are denied on behalf and the allegations are denied. The allegations have been denied on behalf. The allegations, however, are denied on the basis of the allegations. The allegations do not constitute the allegations of mala fide. The allegations cannot be said to be mala fide. [319 E F] The allegations are not vague and do not constitute any allegation of mala fides or mala fides. The allegations must be such as to show that they are mala fide. It is not the case of mala fides that the allegations are mala fide or that they are made with mala fide. They are not vague. The allegations made in the writ application are not vague but do not constitute a charge of mala fides and are not vague or do not constitute an allegation of mala fide or mala fides, and the allegations cannot be regarded as vague. The appellants were convicted under section 395 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to 5 years rigorous imprisonment and fine. The High Court and the Court below were of the opinion that the appellants were themselves the dacoits, and convicted them under section 395. The High court and the Court were of the view that the presumption under section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act was not drawn from the circumstances of the case and that the presumption that they were dacoits was not drawn when the circumstances were proved. The High. Court and the courts below were of opinion that the presumption was not drawn on the circumstances of each case. The High 'Court and the Court found that the appellants had been convicted under section 396 of the Indian IPC and sentenced them to 5 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 100/ . The High Court also held that the appellants could not be convicted under section 397 of the Indian Code. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) The presumption that they are dacoits was only a presumption which could be drawn from the proved circumstances of the particular case. The presumption that the accused was involved in the crime was not drawn by the prosecution and the evidence on which the presumption could be drawn was not drawn in the case. The appellants were not convicted under section 412 of the Indian , and were therefore not liable to be convicted under that section. [723 F G] (ii) The presumption under section 113 of the Evidence Act was drawn from the facts of the case. [724 F] (iii) The presumption was not discharged by the prosecution. The presumption under the section was drawn from those facts. The presumption was drawn from circumstances which the one presumption or the other may be drawn. The presumption could be rebutted only by the evidence of the witnesses who were the dacoits. The presumption is stronger when the discovery of the fruits of crime is made immediately after the crime is committed. The reasons are obvious. Disposal of the fruits, of crime requires the finding of a person ready to receive them and the shortness of time the nature of the property which is disposed of, that is to say, its quantity and its character determined whether the person who had the goods in his possession received them from another or was himself the thief or the dacoit. [725 F G]

The petitioners challenged the validity of Section 5 of the (12 of 1919) (Act No. XIV of 1919), by a writ petition under Article 32 of the Constitution. The petitioners contended that the impugned provisions of the Act were violative of the fundamental rights guaranteed by Article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution and that the impugned provision was violative of the right guaranteed under Article 19(i)(g) and (2) of the constitution. The petitioners also contended that the Act was a Central enactment and that the Act did not violate the fundamental rights of the petitioners. The petitioners further contended that the provisions of the impugned Act were violative and that the provisions were violative of Article 19(6) of the (7) of the Constitutional. The petitioners, therefore, prayed for a writ of mandamus directing the respondents to declare the impugned provisions as unconstitutional and to declare the provisions of section 5 of the Act as unconstitutional and void. The respondents contended that the petitioners were not entitled to the benefit of the Act and that the petitioners had not challenged the vires of the Act. The respondents also contended that they had not placed any matter before the authorities under the Act and the High Court was not justified in holding that the impugned Act was violative of Article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as the Act was not a Central enactment but a State enactment. Dismissing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The impugned provisions are violative of the constitutional rights guaranteed by the Constitution and are, therefore, violative of the rights guaranteed by Part III of the Constitution, and are, accordingly, struck down. [223E] 2. The impugned Act is not violative of the equality clause of the Constitution because it is a State enactment and is not a State enactment, and the impugned Act is a State legislation. [223F] 3. The impugned provision is not violative or arbitrary. It is not necessary that the impugned statute is a State Act. [223G] 4. The impugned statute is not a Central Act but a State Act, and the State Act is a Central Act. The State Act is not a Union Act. The impugned legislation is not a law made by the State Legislature. The impugned enactment is not a legislation within the meaning of Article 12 of the Constitution as it is a Central enactment. [223B]

The appellant was detained under the Bombay Police Act, 1950, on the 8th June 1955, and was in detention for a period of two years. He was in the Indian Air Force as an emergency Commissioned Officer. He was served with a notice on the 1st July 1955, under section 7 of the Act, on the ground that he was not furnished with the grounds of detention. The grounds of detention were vague. The grounds were vague. They were vague. It was contended that the grounds of the detention were vague and that the grounds were vague and the grounds were not vague. Held, that the grounds did not disclose any material to the detenu at the time when the grounds were furnished. The grounds did not indicate any material to justify the detention. The order of detention was mala fide. The last two had been stated to be communicated to the detenu. The order was not a mere communication of the decision to the detenu but was a mere communication to the detenu, at the time of the making of the order. The order did not disclose the material to the detenue at the time. The order, therefore, was not a notice to the detenu and was not a communication to him. The order could not be said to have prejudiced the detenu. It was not a case of a mere communication. The order merely stated that it was made by the detenue at his own request and was not communicated to him. It was a mere order of detention. It was an order of detention made by the Government of Bombay under the Act. The order must be communicated to him within a reasonable time. The fact that the detenue was furnished with the order of detention did not make the order of the detention invalid. The order made by the State Government was not a ' communication to the detenue ' within the meaning of section 3(1) of the Act.

The appellant was a Panchayat Samiti constituted under the C.P. and Berar Panchayat Act, 1946. On July 14, 1961, the Panchayat passed resolution to levy the octroi duty. The resolution was passed by the Panchayat. The resolution, after reciting the need for levying octroi duty, was passed. The resolution also stated that the Panchayat shall be satisfied that the goods brought by it were being used for the purpose of consumption, use or sale within the octroi limits. The resolution further stated that the tax shall be imposed on the goods brought within its local limits as per the Schedule No. 1 of the Rules. The appellant was deemed to be a Panchayat under the Act. On July 15, 1961 the Panchayat passed a resolution to levy octroi duty on the goods coming within its local jurisdiction as per the schedule No. 1. The resolution stated that the octroi duty shall be imposed by the Panchayat on the goods falling within its local area as per the Schedules No. 1 and 2. The appellant filed objections against the proposed levy of octroi duty. On the objections of the appellant, the Panchayat held that the octroi was leviable on the goods which were brought within its territorial limits as per Schedule No. I of the Rules and that the appellant was not liable to pay octroi duty. In the appeal to the Samiti, the appellant contended that the Panchayat was not liable for the levy of octroi duties because the appellant had not produced the goods within the local limits as required by the Schedule No 1 of the Act. The Samiti was not a party to the resolution passed by the Samiti and that the resolution was not a decision of the Panchayat. Held, that the resolution passed in the Samiti was not an order of the Panchayat but was a decision of a Panchayat. The Panchayat was not a body corporate and the resolution was a decision by a Panchayat. It was not a resolution of the Panchayat which was not a 'decision of the Panchayat '. The resolution did not contain any discussion of the question whether the Panchayat was a decision or not of the Panchayat, but was a resolution of a Panchayat which was a decision. The resolution passed in a Panchayat was not an 'decision of a Panchayat ' within the meaning of section 124(5) of the Act and was not a "decision of the panchayat". The resolution was not an "decision of a panchayat" within the meaning Of section 124(6) of the Panchayat Act. The resolution dated July 15,1961 was not a final decision of the panchayat. The resolution of the Samiti was a decision which was not an authority within the meaning ofs.124(5) and was not an administrative decision. The decision of the Samiti in the present case was not a judicial decision within the meaningof section 124(7) of the C. P. and Berar Municipalities Act, 1947. The resolution in question was not a judgment of the Panchayat and was not therefore a decision of an administrative decision within the contemplation of section 124 (5) of Act.

The appellant No. 1, a contractor, was dismissed by the Conciliation Officer on January 9, 1952, and the order of dismissal was confirmed by the State Government on the ground that the conciliation proceedings had continued for a period of more than 14 days as from January 17, 1952. The appellant filed a complaint against the workmen for an offence under section 31(1) read with section 33 of the . The Chief Presidency Magistrate acquitted the appellant on the ground of delay and convicted him under section 31 (1) readwith section 33 of that Act. The High Court, on appeal, reversed the acquittal and convicted the appellant under section 31 of the Act. Held, that the conciliation proceeding could not be said to be pending when the report of the Conciliation Officer was received by the appropriate Government. The conciliation proceedings could be prolonged beyond what was contemplated by the Act and the termination would depend upon what soon a report is received by the Conciliation officer. The conciliation proceeding could be prolonged only when the report is received and the proceedings are not closed. The conciliation Proceedings could be prolonged much beyond what was envisaged by the Act. The conciliation was not a mere formality but a mere formality. The termination of the conciliation proceedings could not be regarded as a mere formality and the proceedings could be continued after the report was received by it. The conciliation officer was not required to bring about settlement within the time prescribed by the Act but when the report was made by the Conciliation Officers within 14 days, the conciliation proceedings were not concluded within the time specified by the Act, and the termination could not affect the closure of the conciliation proceeding. The conciliation enquiry could be prolonged even beyond what was stipulated by the Act or the termination would be a mere formality, and the proceedings did not automatically come to an end after 14 days but only terminate as provided in section 20(2)(b) of the Act and not terminate as provided under section 20(1) of the .

The appellant was appointed as a clerk on an ad hoc basis. He was confirmed in the post of a Head Clerk on an adhoc basis. On April 1, 1975, the appellant was promoted as a Head Clerk. On April 25, 1975 the appellant was appointed to the post of Head Clerk. The Punjab Panchayat Samitis, Zilla Parishads (Haryana Amendment) Act, 1973 introduced extensive amendments in the Act of 1961. Section 13 of the Amending Act deleted section 33 of the Act. A plain consequence of this deletion was that the Panchayat Samitis were divested of their power to make appointments to the Panchayat. The Amending Act received the assent of the Governor on April 25,1973 and was published in the Haryana Gazette on June 13, 1973. Sections 35(1) and (3) of the Amending act, 1973 inserted in section 14(4) of the Act by the Amending Act of 1973. Section 14(4), which dealt with the conditions of service of the Government servants allotted to the Panchayat Samitis was amended by section 14 of the Amending. The Amending Acts were repealed by section 14(1) of the amending Act of 1974. Section 14 of the amending act was deleted by section 14 (4) of 1973 Act. The appellant was appointed a clerk on April 1,1975. On April 28, 1975 he was promoted as Head Clerk on ad hoc basis in January 1974, and on April 1. 1975 he became a Head Clerk in the Loharu Panchayat Samiti. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the Amending Acts. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Panchayat Samiti lost its power to make appointment to the Panchayat, that the appellant was entitled to be absorbed as a Head clerk in any event, and that the appellant had no right to be absorbed in the post. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The right to be considered for promotion is a term and condition of service, which, if it is found that the appellant has been appointed to the posts in the Government, the Government is not bound to absorb him in the post, of a Head clerk. [738A B] 2. The right of the appellant to be considered in promotion is a terms and condition of the service, which is relevant for the purpose of promotion. The fact that the appellant is promoted as a head clerk on an adhoc basis in January, 1974, cannot improve his position for the simple reason that these appointments were made after June 13,1973. [739C D] 3. The right conferred on the appellant by section 14 is a term of service, and the appellant cannot be considered to be a member of the Panchayat Samiti. [740C D]

The appellants were allotted land in the village of Thana in 1949. Their father was the owner of the land in question. The land allotted to them was out of the land released upon the cancellation of allotment in their favour by the order dated October 31, 1952. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General, Evacuee Property, Punjab, under section 19 of the Act, for the restoration of the land to the 14 allottees. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the revision application on the ground that the allotment was not in accordance with the rules of the evacuee property Rules, and that the allotment had been wrongly made. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General. The Custodian General, on the other hand, dismissed the appeal on the ground of delay. The appellants then filed a revision petition before the Custodian, General, for the State of Punjab, for the order cancelling the allotment of the land. The Additional Director of Evacuee Property, however, rejected the revision application and held that the allotment of land was not in conformity with the rules. The appellants appealed to the Custodian, who dismissed the revision petition. The Additional Deputy Custodian, however dismissed the revision. The appellants ' revision petition was dismissed by the Custodian General on the ground, inter alia, that the allotment in favour of the appellants was in contravention of the rules of evacuee property Rules and that the order of the Additional Custodian was not in compliance with the rules and that the orders of the Additional Director of the Evacuee Property were not in accordance With the rules. Held, that the order was not in contravention of section 12 of the Act. The order of the Custodian General was not in violation of the rules. It was not in breach of the rules and was not in excess of the powers conferred by section 19(1) of the Act and was therefore not in contravention with the rules, and was therefore void. The order was not liable to be set aside.

The respondent, a citizen of India, was assessed to income tax for the years 1943 44 to 1947, and a recovery certificate was issued by the Income tax Officer on the 7th June 1955. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the assessment on the ground that the assessment was invalid because the respondent had not paid the assessed amount of tax. The High Court dismissed the petition. The High court held that the assessment order was invalid because it was passed in the public interest and was not a valid order. The High 'Court held that the respondent was not liable to pay the tax. The respondent appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the assessment of the respondent was invalid because, the respondent had failed to pay the assessed tax. The assessment order was not invalid because the assessment was made in the public interests and was not in the interests of the public. The respondent was not entitled to claim any tax on the ground of the assessment. The assessment was made by the Income Tax Officer on the 8th June 1954 and the sale was held on the 25th February 1955 and the sale proceeds were insufficient to satisfy the assessed tax the Additional Collector on the 7. June 1955, issued a notice under section 13 of the Bombay City Land Revenue Act, 1876, requiring the assessee to appear before him in person on the 16th June 1956 and show cause why he should not be apprehended and confined to civil jail in satisfaction of the certified demand. The assessment of the Income tax officer was made on the 7 th June 1955 and was made on that date. The assessment proceedings were therefore invalid. The High Courts were not justified in holding that the assessment made by the respondent was valid because the assessment order did not specify the period of detention of the respondent. The assessment orders were therefore invalid because the order did not contain any reason for the delay in making the assessment.

The appellant, a lessee of a private land, was granted a lease of the land in dispute for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On January 10, 1947 the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease granted by the Rajah to him. The appellant contended that the lease was not a lease within the meaning of the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act, and that the lease could not be terminated by the Government on the expiry of the fifth year. Held, that the appellant was not entitled to the renewal of the lease under r. 47 of the Mineral Concession Rules of 1949. The second proviso to the section, which is a self contained proviso, is not a self contained provision and the aid of the third proviso is wholly uncalled for. The second condition is that the lessee should have the right to terminate the lease and the lessee should be entitled to the same conditions in the second proviso itself. The second part of the proviso deals with the termination of rights created after July 1, 1945, and the second part of r. 47 deals with the continuance of rights created before July 1,1945, and is not void as against the Government. The second clause of the second part deals with the continuation of rights created prior to July 1, of 1945, which was not the subject of the second clause. The second portion of r. 48 deals with the renewal of leases granted by the Government. In other words, the second part dealing with the renewal clause is not applicable to the renewal clause. The third part of r, 48 deals with renewal of leases for a period exceeding one year. The second is not applicable in the present case.
